name: Patch-level Contrastive Learning (e.g., DINO)
analogy: Think of it as a student shown only a few bars of a chart, who must say what kind of session it is. A teacher who sees the whole session gives the answer, and the student learns to name the session from a fragment. Over time the student learns what each piece of a session implies about the whole.

steps.title: Cut each window into patches
steps.description: A long window of bars is divided into short, non-overlapping patches, the way an image is divided into tiles. Each patch is embedded as a unit, and a transformer then lets patches look at one another.
steps.inExample: A 96-bar MNQ window is cut into 12 patches of 8 five-minute bars.

steps.title: Make big views and small views
steps.description: From each window the method builds a few large views covering most of the session, and several small views covering only a part. Altering tricks such as noise or masking can be added on top.
steps.inExample: Each window yields 2 large views of 80 bars and 6 small views of 24 bars.

steps.title: Teacher reads the large views, student reads everything
steps.description: The teacher network sees only the large views. The student network sees both large and small views. The teacher is a slow-moving average of the student, so it changes gradually and is not directly trained.
steps.inExample: The teacher reads the 2 large views; the student reads all 8 views.

steps.title: Turn each output into a distribution over prototype types
steps.description: Each network's output is converted into a probability spread over a fixed number of learned categories, which can be thought of as session types that the model invents for itself. A temperature controls how sharp the spread is.
steps.inExample: Each view is scored against 64 learned session types and the scores become a spread of probabilities.

steps.title: Make the student agree with the teacher
steps.description: The student is adjusted so that its spread, from a small view, matches the teacher's spread from a large view of the same window. No other windows are used as wrong answers. A centring step on the teacher's outputs prevents all windows from collapsing into one type.
steps.inExample: A student that sees only 24 bars learns to put its probability on the same session type as the teacher who sees 80 bars.

steps.title: Read the patch attention afterwards
steps.description: The transformer's attention shows which patches it relied on. Patches the teacher attends to when naming a session are the ones that carry the most information about it.
steps.inExample: For today's window, attention concentrates on the opening patch and the two most recent patches.

useFor.task: Pretraining on long sessions without labels
useFor.example: Learning from years of MNQ sessions cut into patches, before fine-tuning a direction model.
Using the 64 learned types as data-driven regime labels, such as trending drift or tight rotation.

useFor.task: Seeing which part of a session matters
useFor.example: Reading the attention to check whether the opening patch drives the model's description of the day.

useFor.task: Predicting the whole from a part
useFor.example: Describing a partly finished session from just its first 24 bars to support an early read.

avoidWhen: Your windows are short, because patches of a few bars carry too little to compare; a simpler summary of the window works better.
You need an interpretable rule that a person can check; the learned types are invented by the model and need to be inspected before they are trusted.

example.scenario: A researcher pretrains DINO-style on 96-bar MNQ windows cut into 12 patches. Midway through a session, the student sees only the first 24 bars and the researcher asks what session type it assigns and how confident it is.

input.summary: One window cut into patches, with a small view of the first 24 bars given to the student.

fields.name: full window length
fields.meaning: A full session window that the teacher sees in large views.

fields.name: patches per full window
fields.meaning: How the window is cut for the transformer.

fields.name: small view given to the student
fields.meaning: The partial session available early in the day.

fields.name: learned session types
fields.meaning: The number of categories the model invents for itself.

output.summary: A spread of probability over learned session types and a description of the window.

fields.name: most likely session type
fields.meaning: The learned category with the highest probability for this partial window.

fields.name: probability on type 17
fields.meaning: How much of the student's probability sits on that category.

fields.name: second most likely type
fields.meaning: The runner-up category, showing the call is not certain.

fields.name: window description
fields.meaning: The reusable summary of the window for later models.

example.reading: A 41 percent top type with a visible runner-up is a soft call, which is appropriate with only a quarter of the session seen. Look at what other windows share type 17 before giving it a meaning. A type is only useful if sessions in it behave differently afterwards, which has to be tested on walk-forward folds.
